name: OpenBCI
origin_detail: Joel Murphy and Conor Russomanno created OpenBCI, an 'open-source brain-computer interface platform', after a successful Kickstarter campaign in late 2013. It is headquartered in Brooklyn, NY.
flagship_projects: Galea multimodal headset (unveiled late 2020; beta pre-orders Aug 2024)
openness_notes: Hardware column. Initial level 3: the original boards and headset were published as open hardware. Four OpenBCI products were OSHWA-certified in Sept 2017, the Ultracortex headset files are GPL-3.0, and the GUI and Cyton library are MIT. Current level 2 is an inference, flagged low confidence. The newest flagship, Galea (EEG, EMG, EDA, PPG and eye-tracking; CES 2023 Innovation Awards), has no public design repository among the OpenBCI GitHub organisation's 17 public repos (10 visible). Galea's own site returned 403. The Ganglion hardware-design repo shows no licence and was last updated Dec 2023. The older boards remain open, which fits 'older models open, new ones closed'.

risk_events: Ganglion price rose from $99 (Kickstarter) to $249.99 and then to $499.00 (Wikipedia).
Wikipedia flags the OpenBCI article for notability, noting that its claims lack independent sources.
2020-2024: the company moved up-market to Galea, a premium multimodal headset partly aimed at XR and defence (Unity Aerospace & Defense award). Beta pre-orders opened Aug 2024.
robustness: OpenBCI is a small private company. The older boards and headset are openly licensed and OSHWA-certified: Ultracortex is GPL-3.0 (412 stars, 150 forks) and the GUI is MIT (986 stars, 330 forks), so research labs can keep replicating and maintaining them without the company. The newer Galea line appears to depend on the company. Funding and finances are not public. Activity continued into 2025 (Cyton library updated 2025-07-28).
physical_science_relevance: OpenBCI hardware is low-cost research-grade EEG/EMG used in neuroscience and BCI research. OpenBCI keeps a list of peer-reviewed publications that used its products (docs.openbci.com links to openbci.com/citations).
openness_effect_assessment: Kickstarter funding, open designs and OSHWA certification built OpenBCI a research and maker community that publishes peer-reviewed work on its hardware. The company then moved up-market with Galea, which won CES 2023 Innovation Awards and appears not to be open. That suggests openness served as the entry and community strategy while the higher-value product is kept closed, like the Prusa and MakerBot pattern but without an acquisition. No financial data were found to measure the effect.
key_takeaway: OpenBCI is the open-science hardware archetype: a crowdfunded (2013) Brooklyn startup whose open EEG boards and GPL-licensed 3D-printable headset made research-grade biosensing affordable. It has stayed small and private, and its recent focus is a premium, apparently closed multimodal headset (Galea) for XR and defence-adjacent markets. Openness created the research user base. Whether it also funds the company could not be determined, because no funding or revenue figures were reachable without search.
